subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If α, β are the roots of the equation x² − 2x + 4 = 0, then show that αⁿ + βⁿ = 2ⁿ⁺¹ cos(nπ/3).

mark_split.label: Find the roots α and β
Raise to n by De Moivre's theorem

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.16 — LAQ chapter 1 De Moivre's Theorem, answer 4. Printed appearances: AP 17,19,19 · TS 16 (the book prints AP 19 twice, presumably two 2019 papers; recorded as two entries). THE 1+2+1+1+2 SPLIT IS THE BOOK'S — book p.16 prints five tags down the answer: [1 Mark] against the roots 1 ± i√3, [2 Marks] against r and tan θ, [1 Mark] against the mod-amp form raised to n, [1 Mark] against equation (1) by De Moivre, and [2 Marks] against the addition; the 'Similarly … (2)' line carries no tag of its own. We keep the printed totals and step order with ONE placement call flagged for the teacher: the fourth tag's mark is put on the conjugate equation (2) rather than as a second mark on equation (1), so the conjugate step is not a 0-mark step and the answer keeps the family's shape. The SAME split shape and the SAME step ids (s1_mod_amp, s2_de_moivre, s3_conjugate, s4_add) are used on answers 1.1, 1.2, 2 and 5 of this unit, deliberately: they are one method (mod-amp form → De Moivre → the conjugate pair → add) over different numbers. Answer 4 carries the same step names shifted by one because the book's own [1 Mark] roots step precedes them. The book's LAQ chapter header (book p.14) carries ★★★ and reads '7 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-2A Section C runs Q18–Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q18 is the De Moivre's Theorem slot (blueprint book p.3 and all five model papers, book pp.111–120). 2A is still the 75-mark pre-reform paper in 2026-27 (the 60-mark reform is first year only), so the LAQ is authored at 7 marks, not re-cut to 8. No two-book union check and no board back-test exist for this paper (no second Maths-2A source in the corpus; answer-book/papers/ holds first-year physics only) — recorded, not hidden. Re-derived: x² − 2x + 4 = 0 gives 1 ± i√3 = 2 cis(±π/3), so αⁿ + βⁿ = 2ⁿ⁺¹ cos(nπ/3); the book's answer is correct. Asked as Model Paper 3, Q18 (book p.116), whose answer-page index prints 'P 15(3)' although this answer is number 4 on book p.16. Re-solved in the Bullet Model Paper Q18 (book p.104) with the same steps.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — how you get α and β, how you write 1 + i√3, what De Moivre's theorem does to it, and how the two powers combine.
insider_note: Five printed mark tags and a four-times-asked question. The one mark most students drop is the first: the roots must be written as 1 ± i√3 before anything else.

steps.label: Find the roots α and β
steps.margin_note: First mark. The discriminant is 4 − 16 = −12, so √(−12) = 2i√3 and x = (2 ± 2i√3)/2 = 1 ± i√3. Divide both terms by 2, not only the first.

recall.must_convey: That the quadratic is solved first and its roots are the conjugate pair 1 ± i√3.
accept: solve the quadratic first, the roots are one plus i root three and one minus i root three
alpha and beta are one plus or minus i root three from the quadratic formula
the discriminant is minus twelve so the roots are one plus minus i root three
quadratic solve cheste alpha beta one plus minus i root three vasthai
the roots are complex conjugates one plus i root three and one minus i root three

steps.why: The question names α and β but never writes them down; nothing can be raised to a power until the roots are found. The negative discriminant is what makes this a De Moivre question at all.
common_mistakes: Simplifying (2 ± 2i√3)/2 to 2 ± i√3 by dividing only the first term.
Stopping at the roots and trying to expand (1 + i√3)ⁿ by the binomial theorem.

steps.label: Mod-amp form of 1 + i√3
steps.margin_note: Second and third marks. For 1 + i√3: r = √(1 + 3) = 2 and tan θ = √3, so θ = π/3, with x and y both positive. That r = 2 outside the bracket is where the 2ⁿ⁺¹ in the answer comes from.
lines: Let 1 + i√3 = x + iy ⇒ x = 1, y = √3

recall.must_convey: That 1 + i√3 is first written in modulus-amplitude form: r = 2 and θ = π/3, giving r(cos θ + i sin θ).
accept: first write 1 + i√3 in mod amp form with r equal to 2 and theta equal to π/3
find the modulus and the amplitude of 1 + i√3 and write it as r cos theta plus i sin theta
convert 1 + i√3 to polar form r cis theta before raising the power
1 + i√3 ni mod amp form lo rasi r 2 theta π/3 teeskovali
modulus amplitude form first, r is 2 and the angle is π/3

steps.why: De Moivre's theorem works only on a number written as cos θ + i sin θ. Pulling out r first is what makes the theorem usable, so this line is the method, not a preliminary.
common_mistakes: Writing r = √3 or r = 4 instead of √(1 + 3) = 2.
Reading tan θ = √3 as θ = π/6; π/6 has tan = 1/√3.
Forgetting the r = 2 outside the bracket, which is where the 2ⁿ comes from.

steps.label: Raise to n by De Moivre
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. αⁿ = 2ⁿ[cos(nπ/3) + i sin(nπ/3)]: the modulus 2 is raised to n as an ordinary real number and the power moves onto the angle inside. Label it (1).
lines: αⁿ = (1 + i√3)ⁿ = [2(cos π/3 + i sin π/3)]ⁿ

recall.must_convey: That De Moivre's theorem is applied: raising the mod-amp form to the power n multiplies the angle by n and gives 2ⁿ(cos(nπ/3) + i sin(nπ/3)), called equation (1).
accept: apply De Moivre's theorem so the angle is multiplied by n and we get 2ⁿ(cos(nπ/3) + i sin(nπ/3))
raise the mod amp form to the power and multiply the angle by n by De Moivre
by De Moivre cos theta plus i sin theta to the power gives cos n theta plus i sin n theta
De Moivre theorem apply chesi angle ni n tho multiply cheyyali
the power goes onto the angle by De Moivre's theorem, that is equation one

steps.why: De Moivre's theorem says (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ for every integer n: the power moves onto the angle. The real factor r is raised separately, as an ordinary real number.
common_mistakes: Raising r to the power but forgetting to multiply the angle by the same power.
Multiplying the angle by the power but leaving r un-raised.
Writing (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cosⁿ θ + i sinⁿ θ, which is false.

steps.label: The conjugate power
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. β = 1 − i√3 is the conjugate of α, so βⁿ has the same 2ⁿ and the same angle with the sine sign reversed. Label it (2); nothing is recomputed.

recall.must_convey: That the conjugate number is treated in the same way and gives 2ⁿ(cos(nπ/3) − i sin(nπ/3)), called equation (2), with the sign of the sine term changed.
accept: similarly the conjugate gives the same thing with minus i sin, that is equation two
do the same for the conjugate and only the sign of the sine changes
the second bracket is the conjugate so its power is 2ⁿ(cos(nπ/3) − i sin(nπ/3))
conjugate ki same step, sin term sign matrame minus avuthundi
equation two is the conjugate with cos minus i sin

steps.why: The second number is the conjugate of the first, so it has the same r and the angle −θ. Nothing new has to be computed; only the sign of the sine changes.
common_mistakes: Changing the sign of the cosine as well as the sine.
Recomputing r and θ from scratch and losing time.
Writing equation (2) without the minus sign, so nothing cancels in the next step.

steps.label: Add (1) and (2)
steps.margin_note: Sixth and seventh marks. Adding (1) and (2) cancels the two i sin terms and doubles the cosine: 2ⁿ · 2 cos(nπ/3). Combine the powers of 2 into 2ⁿ⁺¹, the form the question asks for.

recall.must_convey: That equations (1) and (2) are added, the i sin terms cancel, and the result is 2ⁿ⁺¹ cos(nπ/3).
accept: add one and two, the i sin terms cancel and we get 2ⁿ⁺¹ cos(nπ/3)
adding the two equations the sine parts cancel leaving two times the cosine
one plus two gives two cos and the final answer is 2ⁿ⁺¹ cos(nπ/3)
rendu equations add cheste sin terms cancel ayyi 2ⁿ⁺¹ cos(nπ/3) vasthundi
the imaginary parts cancel on adding and the answer is two to the n plus one times cos

steps.why: The two numbers are conjugates, so their sum is twice the real part. Adding removes the i sin terms and leaves exactly the cosine the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Subtracting instead of adding, which leaves 2i sin instead of 2 cos.
Leaving the answer as 2ⁿ · 2 cos instead of combining into one power of 2.
Dropping the factor that comes from r, which is the whole reason the answer has a power of 2.
